title: How Chinese characters work
examples: How many Chinese characters are there?

stages.label: 林 lín: woods

explain.say: English uses 26 letters to spell sounds. Chinese does something different: each character stands for a whole word or part of a word, with its own meaning. Look at the board: hanzi, han, zi, means Chinese characters. Ready to read your first one?

Look at the first box: 木, said mù, which means tree. Can you see it? A trunk, branches reaching up, and roots spreading down. Some of the oldest characters began as little pictures, called pictographs.

explain.say: Now watch the next box: 林, lín. Two trees side by side. What do you get? Woods! And look at the third box: 森, sēn, three trees. A forest! Characters can be built from smaller pieces. What would you guess four trees means?

explain.say: See the last box? 休, xiū, means rest. On the left is a small form of the character for person. On the right, a tree. A person leaning against a tree... is resting! Isn't that clever? Many characters mix a meaning part and a sound part.

explain.say: Amazing reading! Chinese is called logographic, which means word-writing. A big dictionary lists tens of thousands of characters, but about 3,000 are enough to read a newspaper. Wow: people who speak very different Chinese languages can read the same characters!

faq.a: Some began as pictures, like 木 for tree and 山 for mountain, but most characters today combine a part that hints at meaning with a part that hints at sound.
Many are made of smaller pieces. 林, woods, is two trees. 休, rest, is a person next to a tree. Parts that show meaning are called radicals.

faq.q: How many Chinese characters are there?
faq.a: Large dictionaries list more than 50,000, but most are rare. About 3,000 common characters cover nearly everything in a newspaper.
asks: How many characters do I need?

faq.a: Logographic means each symbol stands for a word or a meaningful part of a word, rather than a single sound.
Pinyin is a way of writing Chinese sounds with Latin letters and tone marks, like mù for 木. Children in China learn it to help them read.

facts: About 3,000 common Chinese characters cover around 99 percent of the characters in everyday texts.
Mainland China uses simplified characters; Taiwan and Hong Kong use traditional ones.
